l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 51. 1. All things are produced by the Tao, and nourished by its
s: This unit concerns the Tao and all things. The Tao produces, nourishes, forms, completes, matures, maintains, and overspreads all things. All things honour the Tao and exalt its outflowing operation through a spontaneous tribute. The Tao does not claim possession, vaunt its ability, or exercise control over what it brings to maturity.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 51. 1. All things are produced by the Tao, and nourished by its
s: The Tao produces, nourishes, forms, completes, matures, maintains, and overspreads all things. It does not claim possession, vaunt its ability, or exercise control over what it brings to maturity.

l: all things, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 51. 1. All things are produced by the Tao, and nourished by its
s: All things receive their forms according to their nature and are completed according to the circumstances of their condition. They honour the Tao and exalt its outflowing operation through a spontaneous tribute.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 52. 1. (The Tao) which originated all under the sky is to be
s: The Tao originated all under the sky and is considered the mother of them all. When the mother is found, one knows what her children should be, and guarding the qualities of the mother keeps one free from peril. Keeping the mouth closed and the portals shut brings exemption from laborious exertion, while promoting affairs through breath brings no safety. Perceiving what is small gives clear-sightedness, and guarding what is soft and tender gives strength; using light well and reverting to its bright source wards off blight and hides the unchanging from men's sight.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 52. 1. (The Tao) which originated all under the sky is to be
s: The Tao originated all under the sky and is considered the mother of them all.

l: mother (The Tao), The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 52. 1. (The Tao) which originated all under the sky is to be
s: The mother is found as the source from which one knows what her children should be. Guarding the qualities of the mother that belong to one keeps one free from all peril to the end of life.

l: children (the mother’s children), The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 52. 1. (The Tao) which originated all under the sky is to be
s: The children are what one comes to know when the mother is found.

l: one, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 52. 1. (The Tao) which originated all under the sky is to be
s: One knows that he is his mother's child and can proceed to guard the qualities of the mother that belong to him. By keeping his mouth closed and shutting up the portals of his nostrils, one remains free from laborious exertion; by keeping his mouth open and promoting his affairs through breath, one has no safety.

l: light, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 52. 1. (The Tao) which originated all under the sky is to be
s: Light is to be used well by reverting to its bright source. Doing so wards all blight from one's body and hides the unchanging from men's sight.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 53. 1. If I were suddenly to become known, and (put into a position
s: The unit concerns governing according to the Great Tao and the dangers of boastful display. It says the Great Tao is level and easy, but people prefer byways. It describes princes who maintain their courts while neglecting fields and granaries, indulge in luxury, and accumulate wealth, calling them robbers and boasters contrary to the Tao.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 53. 1. If I were suddenly to become known, and (put into a position
s: The Great Tao is described as a very level and easy way. Conducting a government according to it is presented as the proper course.

l: government, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 53. 1. If I were suddenly to become known, and (put into a position
s: A government may be conducted according to the Great Tao. Someone in such a position would be most afraid of a boastful display.

l: people, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 53. 1. If I were suddenly to become known, and (put into a position
s: People love the byways even though the Great Tao is level and easy.

l: princes, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 53. 1. If I were suddenly to become known, and (put into a position
s: Princes keep their courts well maintained but leave their fields ill-cultivated and their granaries nearly empty. They wear elegant robes, carry sharp swords, pamper themselves with food and drink, and possess excessive property and wealth.

l: robbers and boasters, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 53. 1. If I were suddenly to become known, and (put into a position
s: Princes who display luxury while neglecting fields and granaries may be called robbers and boasters. Their conduct is contrary to the Tao.

l: boastful display, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 53. 1. If I were suddenly to become known, and (put into a position
s: Boastful display is identified as what someone conducting a government according to the Great Tao should be most afraid of.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 54.
s: This unit concerns Tao and its effects when cultivated within a person, family, neighbourhood, state, and kingdom. Tao is compared to skilful planting and careful cultivation that cannot be uprooted or taken away. When Tao prevails, families gain riches, neighbourhoods thrive, states find good fortune, and people prosper throughout the kingdom. The text says this effect is confirmed by observing different cases under the sky.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 54.
s: Tao is compared to what a skilful planter plants and what skilful arms enfold, which cannot be uprooted or taken away. When nursed within a person, Tao makes that person's vigour true; when applied through the family, neighbourhood, state, and kingdom, it brings increasing prosperity and good fortune.

l: family, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 54.
s: When Tao rules the family, riches accrue. Sons bring in a lengthening line of sacrifices to the shrine.

l: neighbourhood, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 54.
s: When Tao prevails in the neighbourhood, the neighbourhood abounds in thriving.

l: state, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 54.
s: When Tao is seen throughout the state, good fortune is found.

l: kingdom, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 54.
s: When Tao is employed throughout the kingdom, men thrive all around.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 55. 1. He who has in himself abundantly the attributes (of the Tao) is
s: He who has in himself abundantly the attributes of the Tao is like an infant. The infant is protected from poisonous insects, fierce beasts, and birds of prey, and its weak bones, soft sinews, firm grasp, excited virile member, and unhoarse crying show the perfection of its physical essence and harmony. Knowing this harmony reveals the unchanging Tao, while all life-increasing arts turn to evil. When things become strong, they become old and soon end because this is contrary to the Tao.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 55. 1. He who has in himself abundantly the attributes (of the Tao) is
s: The unchanging Tao is revealed through knowledge of the harmony shown by the infant. Becoming strong and old is contrary to the Tao.

l: he who has in himself abundantly the attributes (of the Tao), The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 55. 1. He who has in himself abundantly the attributes (of the Tao) is
s: He who has in himself abundantly the attributes of the Tao is like an infant.

l: infant, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 55. 1. He who has in himself abundantly the attributes (of the Tao) is
s: The infant is not stung by poisonous insects, seized by fierce beasts, or struck by birds of prey. Its weak bones and soft sinews coexist with a firm grasp, an excited virile member, and crying that does not make its throat hoarse, showing the perfection of its physical essence and harmony.

l: harmony, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 55. 1. He who has in himself abundantly the attributes (of the Tao) is
s: Harmony is shown by the infant's ability to cry all day without its throat becoming hoarse. Knowing this harmony reveals the unchanging Tao.

l: strength, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 55. 1. He who has in himself abundantly the attributes (of the Tao) is
s: When the mind makes the vital breath burn, the strength is false and should be mourned. When things have become strong, they become old, contrary to the Tao.

l: becoming strong and old, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 55. 1. He who has in himself abundantly the attributes (of the Tao) is
s: Becoming strong and old is contrary to the Tao, and whatever is contrary to the Tao soon ends.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 56. 1. He who knows (the Tao) does not (care to) speak (about it); he
s: The unit concerns the Tao and the person who knows it. A knower of the Tao does not speak about it, keeps his mouth shut, closes the portals of his nostrils, and harmonizes himself with obscurity. This state of blunting sharp points, unraveling complications, attempering brightness, and agreeing with obscurity is called the Mysterious Agreement, and the person who embodies it is beyond ordinary distinctions and is the noblest man under heaven.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 56. 1. He who knows (the Tao) does not (care to) speak (about it); he
s: The Tao is known by a person who does not speak about it. The text presents knowledge of the Tao as involving silence and inward harmony.

l: knower of the Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 56. 1. He who knows (the Tao) does not (care to) speak (about it); he
s: The knower of the Tao keeps his mouth shut and closes the portals of his nostrils. He blunts his sharp points, unravels the complications of things, attempers his brightness, and brings himself into agreement with the obscurity of others; he is beyond familiarity, distance, profit, injury, nobility, and meanness.

l: Mysterious Agreement, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 56. 1. He who knows (the Tao) does not (care to) speak (about it); he
s: The Mysterious Agreement is the name for blunting sharp points, unraveling complications, attempering brightness, and bringing oneself into agreement with the obscurity of others.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 57. 1. A state may be ruled by (measures of) correction; weapons of
s: The unit concerns how a state and kingdom are governed. It says that correction and weapons may rule a state, and crafty dexterity may be used in war, but a kingdom becomes one's own through freedom from action and purpose. It explains that prohibitive enactments, implements for profit, crafty acts, and legislation bring poverty, disorder, strange contrivances, and thieves and robbers. A sage teaches that doing nothing of purpose, keeping still, avoiding trouble, and showing no ambition allow the people to become correct, rich, and primitively simple.

l: state, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 57. 1. A state may be ruled by (measures of) correction; weapons of
s: A state may be ruled by measures of correction, and weapons of war may be used with crafty dexterity.

l: kingdom, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 57. 1. A state may be ruled by (measures of) correction; weapons of
s: A kingdom is made one's own only by freedom from action and purpose. When prohibitive enactments and legislation increase, the kingdom experiences greater poverty, disorder, and theft.

l: people, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 57. 1. A state may be ruled by (measures of) correction; weapons of
s: The people become poor as prohibitive enactments multiply. According to the sage, they will become correct, rich, and attain primitive simplicity when he does nothing of purpose, keeps still, takes no trouble, and manifests no ambition.

l: sage, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 57. 1. A state may be ruled by (measures of) correction; weapons of
s: The sage says that he will do nothing of purpose, keep still, take no trouble, and manifest no ambition. He teaches that these actions allow the people to transform themselves, become correct, become rich, and attain primitive simplicity.

l: freedom from action and purpose, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 57. 1. A state may be ruled by (measures of) correction; weapons of
s: Freedom from action and purpose is presented as the means by which a kingdom is made one's own.

l: crafty dexterity, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 57. 1. A state may be ruled by (measures of) correction; weapons of
s: Crafty dexterity may be used with weapons of war. As men possess more acts of crafty dexterity, more strange contrivances appear.

l: prohibitive enactments, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 57. 1. A state may be ruled by (measures of) correction; weapons of
s: The multiplication of prohibitive enactments increases the poverty of the people.

l: poverty, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 57. 1. A state may be ruled by (measures of) correction; weapons of
s: Poverty among the people increases when prohibitive enactments multiply.

l: disorder, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 57. 1. A state may be ruled by (measures of) correction; weapons of
s: Disorder in the state and clan increases as the people acquire more implements to add to their profit.

l: legislation, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 57. 1. A state may be ruled by (measures of) correction; weapons of
s: The more display there is of legislation, the more thieves and robbers there are.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 58.
s: The unit concerns government, correction, and the sage’s conduct. It says that government which meddles in everything often works ill, while seemingly unwise government may best supply goodness to the people. It explains that correction can turn into distortion and good into evil, amid persistent public delusion. The sage acts like a harmless square or corner: straightforward without license and bright without dazzling.

l: government, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 58.
s: Government that seems most unwise may best supply goodness to the people. Government that meddles with everything works poorly and brings disappointment.

l: people, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 58.
s: The people are subject to changing conditions in which misery and happiness accompany or conceal one another. Their delusion about correction and distortion has persisted for a long time.

l: correction, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 58.
s: Correction may by a turn become distortion, and the good within it may become evil.

l: sage, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 58.
s: The sage is harmless and does not injure others with sharpness or angles. He is straightforward without allowing himself license, and bright without dazzling.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 59. 1. For regulating the human (in our constitution) and rendering
s: The unit concerns moderation in regulating the human (in our constitution) and rendering proper service to the heavenly. Moderation effects an early return to man's normal state, which is described as the repeated accumulation of the attributes of the Tao. That repeated accumulation brings the subjugation of every obstacle to such return, whose limit is unknown. One who possesses the mother of the state may continue long, with deep roots and firm flower stalks securing enduring life.

l: moderation, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 59. 1. For regulating the human (in our constitution) and rendering
s: Moderation regulates the human (in our constitution) and renders the proper service to the heavenly. It effects an early return to man's normal state.

l: the human (in our constitution), The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 59. 1. For regulating the human (in our constitution) and rendering
s: The human (in our constitution) is regulated by moderation.

l: early return (to man's normal state), The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 59. 1. For regulating the human (in our constitution) and rendering
s: The early return to man's normal state is effected by moderation. It is the repeated accumulation of the attributes of the Tao.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 59. 1. For regulating the human (in our constitution) and rendering
s: The Tao is associated with attributes that are repeatedly accumulated in the early return to man's normal state.

l: attributes of the Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 59. 1. For regulating the human (in our constitution) and rendering
s: The attributes of the Tao are repeatedly accumulated in the early return to man's normal state. Their repeated accumulation brings the subjugation of every obstacle to such return.

l: subjugation (of every obstacle to such return), The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 59. 1. For regulating the human (in our constitution) and rendering
s: The subjugation of every obstacle to such return comes from the repeated accumulation of the attributes of the Tao. Its limit is unknown.

l: ruler of a state, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 59. 1. For regulating the human (in our constitution) and rendering
s: One who does not know what the limit of the subjugation shall be may be the ruler of a state.

l: state, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 59. 1. For regulating the human (in our constitution) and rendering
s: The state is associated with the ruler who may arise through not knowing the limit of the subjugation. Possessing the mother of the state allows one to continue long.

l: mother of the state, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 59. 1. For regulating the human (in our constitution) and rendering
s: The mother of the state is possessed by one who may continue long. Its case is compared to a plant with deep roots and firm flower stalks, securing enduring life.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 60. 1. Governing a great state is like cooking small fish.
s: The unit compares governing a great state to cooking small fish. It says the kingdom should be governed according to the Tao so that the manes of the departed do not manifest or employ their spiritual energy to hurt men. Neither the manes nor the ruling sage injuriously affect each other, and their good influences converge in the virtue of the Tao.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 60. 1. Governing a great state is like cooking small fish.
s: The Tao provides the way according to which the kingdom should be governed.

l: kingdom, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 60. 1. Governing a great state is like cooking small fish.
s: The great state is compared to small fish being cooked, implying that it should be governed carefully.

l: manes of the departed, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 60. 1. Governing a great state is like cooking small fish.
s: When the kingdom is governed according to the Tao, the manes of the departed do not manifest their spiritual energy. They do not employ that energy to hurt men.

l: spiritual energy, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 60. 1. Governing a great state is like cooking small fish.
s: The spiritual energy of the manes of the departed exists but is not manifested or employed to hurt men when the kingdom is governed according to the Tao.

l: men, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 60. 1. Governing a great state is like cooking small fish.
s: Men are not hurt by the spiritual energy of the manes of the departed, and the ruling sage does not hurt them.

l: sage, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 60. 1. Governing a great state is like cooking small fish.
s: The ruling sage does not injuriously affect the manes of the departed or hurt men.

l: good influences, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 60. 1. Governing a great state is like cooking small fish.
s: The good influences of the manes of the departed and the ruling sage converge when they do not injuriously affect each other.

l: virtue of the Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 60. 1. Governing a great state is like cooking small fish.
s: The virtue of the Tao is where the good influences converge when the manes of the departed and the ruling sage do not injuriously affect each other.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 61. 1. What makes a great state is its being (like) a low-lying,
s: The unit explains that a great state resembles a low-lying, down-flowing stream toward which the small states tend. It compares this principle to the female overcoming the male through stillness, which is treated as a kind of abasement. A great state gains small states by condescending to them, while small states win over a great state by abasing themselves. The great state seeks to unite and nourish people, while a small state seeks acceptance and service, and the great state must learn to abase itself.

l: kingdom, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 61. 1. What makes a great state is its being (like) a low-lying,
s: The great state is compared to a low-lying, down-flowing stream that becomes the center toward which the small states tend. By condescending to small states, it gains them for itself, and it seeks to unite and nourish people. It must learn to abase itself.

l: small states, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 61. 1. What makes a great state is its being (like) a low-lying,
s: The small states tend toward the great state as toward a low-lying, down-flowing stream. By abasing themselves to a great state, they win it over and seek to be received by and serve it.

l: female, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 61. 1. What makes a great state is its being (like) a low-lying,
s: The female is used as an example of overcoming the male through stillness.

l: stillness, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 61. 1. What makes a great state is its being (like) a low-lying,
s: Stillness enables the female to overcome the male. It may be considered a sort of abasement.

l: abasement, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 61. 1. What makes a great state is its being (like) a low-lying,
s: Abasement is associated with stillness and produces different results depending on who practices it. For a great state it leads to gaining adherents, while for a small state it leads to procuring favour.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 62.
s: This unit concerns Tao and its honored place among all things. Its admirable words can purchase honour, and its admirable deeds can raise their performer above others, while it also guards bad men and effaces their ill. The sovereign, as the Son of Heaven, appoints three ducal ministers, yet an offering of great rank would be less valuable than a lesson of Tao. The ancients prized Tao because it could be obtained by seeking and could allow the guilty to escape their guilt, which is why all under heaven consider it most valuable.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 62.
s: Tao has the most honoured place of all things. Its admirable words can purchase honour, its admirable deeds can raise their performer above others, and it guards bad men while effacing their ill. A lesson of Tao is more valuable than a great symbol-of-rank offering, and it can be obtained by seeking and allow the guilty to escape their guilt.

l: the sovereign, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 62.
s: The sovereign occupies his place as the Son of Heaven and appoints his three ducal ministers. Even in that position, a great offering presented to him would not equal a lesson of Tao.

l: all under heaven, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 62.
s: All under heaven consider Tao the most valuable thing because it can be obtained by seeking and can allow the guilty to escape their guilt.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 63. 1. (It is the way of the Tao) to act without (thinking of) acting;
s: This unit concerns the way of the Tao and the conduct of the sage. The way of the Tao is to act without thinking of acting, conduct affairs without trouble, treat the small as great and a few as many, and recompense injury with kindness. The sage anticipates difficulty while things are easy and accomplishes great things by acting while they are still small. The unit teaches that difficult and great things arise from earlier easy and small states, and that the sage avoids difficulty by recognizing it even in what seems easy.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 63. 1. (It is the way of the Tao) to act without (thinking of) acting;
s: The Tao is associated with acting without thinking of acting, conducting affairs without trouble, tasting without discerning flavour, treating the small as great and a few as many, and recompensing injury with kindness.

l: the way of the Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 63. 1. (It is the way of the Tao) to act without (thinking of) acting;
s: The way of the Tao is to act without thinking of acting and to conduct affairs without feeling their trouble. It also teaches treating what is small as great, a few as many, and recompensing injury with kindness.

l: sage, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 63. 1. (It is the way of the Tao) to act without (thinking of) acting;
s: The sage anticipates difficult things while they are easy and does things that would become great while they are small. By never doing what is great, the sage is able to accomplish the greatest things, and by seeing difficulty even in what seems easy, the sage avoids difficulties.

l: injury, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 63. 1. (It is the way of the Tao) to act without (thinking of) acting;
s: In the way of the Tao, injury is recompensed with kindness.

l: kindness, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 63. 1. (It is the way of the Tao) to act without (thinking of) acting;
s: Kindness is given in recompense for injury.

l: difficulty, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 63. 1. (It is the way of the Tao) to act without (thinking of) acting;
s: Difficulty arises from a previous state in which things were easy. The sage sees difficulty even in what seems easy and therefore never has difficulties.

l: greatness, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 63. 1. (It is the way of the Tao) to act without (thinking of) acting;
s: Great things arise from a previous state in which they were small. The sage accomplishes the greatest things by acting before things become great.

l: smallness, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 63. 1. (It is the way of the Tao) to act without (thinking of) acting;
s: Small things are treated as great in the way of the Tao. The sage does things while they are small, before they become great.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 64. 1. That which is at rest is easily kept hold of; before a thing
s: The unit explains that things are easiest to control before they appear, become disorderly, or approach failure. It teaches that great structures and journeys begin from small beginnings. It says that acting with an ulterior purpose causes harm and that people often ruin affairs when they are near success. The sage avoids such action, desires what other men do not, learns what they do not, and supports the natural development of all things.

l: that which is at rest, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 64. 1. That which is at rest is easily kept hold of; before a thing
s: That which is at rest is easily kept hold of.

l: thing, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 64. 1. That which is at rest is easily kept hold of; before a thing
s: A thing is easiest to address before it gives indications of its presence. A brittle thing is easily broken, and a very small thing is easily dispersed.

l: action, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 64. 1. That which is at rest is easily kept hold of; before a thing
s: Action should be taken before a thing has made its appearance.

l: order, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 64. 1. That which is at rest is easily kept hold of; before a thing
s: Order should be secured before disorder has begun.

l: disorder, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 64. 1. That which is at rest is easily kept hold of; before a thing
s: Disorder is something that should be prevented before it begins.

l: sage, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 64. 1. That which is at rest is easily kept hold of; before a thing
s: The sage does not act with an ulterior purpose and therefore does no harm. The sage does not lay hold of things in that way and therefore does not lose his hold. He desires what other men do not desire, does not prize things difficult to get, learns what other men do not learn, and turns back to what the multitude of men have passed by.

l: people, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 64. 1. That which is at rest is easily kept hold of; before a thing
s: People in their conduct of affairs are constantly ruining them when they are on the eve of success.

l: affairs, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 64. 1. That which is at rest is easily kept hold of; before a thing
s: Affairs are often ruined by people when they are on the eve of success. They would not be so ruined if people were careful at the end as they are at the beginning.

l: success, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 64. 1. That which is at rest is easily kept hold of; before a thing
s: Success is a point at which people often ruin their affairs when they are on its eve.

l: beginning, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 64. 1. That which is at rest is easily kept hold of; before a thing
s: The beginning is the point at which care should be exercised if affairs are not to be ruined at the end.

l: other men, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 64. 1. That which is at rest is easily kept hold of; before a thing
s: Other men desire things that the sage does not desire and prize things difficult to get. They learn what the sage does not learn.

l: multitude of men, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 64. 1. That which is at rest is easily kept hold of; before a thing
s: The multitude of men has passed by what the sage turns back to.

l: natural development of all things, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 64. 1. That which is at rest is easily kept hold of; before a thing
s: The sage helps the natural development of all things and does not dare to act with an ulterior purpose of his own.

l: all things, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 64. 1. That which is at rest is easily kept hold of; before a thing
s: All things undergo a natural development that the sage helps.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 65. 1. The ancients who showed their skill in practising the Tao did
s: The ancients who practised the Tao sought to make the people simple and ignorant rather than enlighten them. The difficulty in governing the people is said to arise from their having much knowledge. Governing a state by wisdom is described as harmful, while not doing so is described as beneficial. The governor who understands these principles follows the model and rule of mysterious excellence, which leads people toward conformity with him.

They would return to knotted cords, value simple food, clothing, dwellings, and ways, and remain isolated from a neighbouring state. Although the neighbouring state would be close enough for its fowls and dogs to be heard, the people would have no intercourse with it even in old age or at death.

l: little state, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 80. 1. In a little state with a small population, I would so order it,
s: The little state has a small population. It is organized so that people have little need for exceptional abilities, vehicles, weapons, or intercourse with neighbouring states.

l: people (little state), The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 80. 1. In a little state with a small population, I would so order it,
s: The people are made to avoid employment of exceptional abilities, travel, and the use of weapons. They return to knotted cords, value coarse food, plain clothes, poor dwellings, and simple ways, and do not communicate with the neighbouring state.

l: death, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 80. 1. In a little state with a small population, I would so order it,
s: The people regard death as a grievous thing. Even so, they are not made to leave elsewhere to avoid it, and they remain without intercourse with the neighbouring state until death.

l: neighbouring state, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 80. 1. In a little state with a small population, I would so order it,
s: The neighbouring state is close enough to be within sight, and the voices of its fowls and dogs can be heard. Despite this proximity, the people have no intercourse with it.

l: intercourse between the states, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 80. 1. In a little state with a small population, I would so order it,
s: There is no intercourse between the little state and the neighbouring state. The people are kept from such intercourse from youth through old age and even until death.

l: The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 81. 1. Sincere words are not fine; fine words are not sincere. Those
s: The unit contrasts sincere words with fine words and describes those skilled in the Tao as non-disputatious, while those who dispute are not skilled in it. It says that those who know the Tao are not extensively learned, and those who are extensively learned do not know it. The sage does not accumulate for himself; by expending and giving to others, he possesses and has more himself. The Way of Heaven injures not, and the sage does not strive in his doing.

l: Tao, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 81. 1. Sincere words are not fine; fine words are not sincere. Those
s: The Tao is associated with skill that does not dispute and with knowledge that is not dependent on extensive learning.

l: sage, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 81. 1. Sincere words are not fine; fine words are not sincere. Those
s: The sage does not accumulate for himself. The more he expends for and gives to others, the more he possesses and has himself; in doing, he does not strive.

l: Way of Heaven, The Tao Teh King, or The Tao and Its Characteristics, 81. 1. Sincere words are not fine; fine words are not sincere. Those
s: The Way of Heaven has all the sharpness yet injures not.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, _Introduction._
s: This unit introduces Chuang Tzŭ, a thinker of the feudal age whose allegorical writings followed Lao Tzŭ and challenged the Confucian and Mihist schools. It explains Lao Tzŭ’s teachings about TAO, or The Way, and especially Inaction, contrasting them with Confucius’s practical ethics and materialism. It discusses the disputed origins, transmission, editing, and classification of Chuang Tzŭ’s work and The Tao-Tê-Ching. It also argues that neither work should properly be treated as a sacred book.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, _Introduction._
s: Chuang Tzŭ belonged to the third and fourth centuries before Christ and held a petty official post at Ch'i-yüan in Mêng. His teachings followed Lao Tzŭ but extended into original philosophical speculations, and he criticized the Confucian and Mihist schools. He refused an invitation to become Prime Minister, choosing freedom over office.

l: the book of Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, _Introduction._
s: Chuang Tzŭ's work is largely allegorical, literary, and dialectical, and it has suffered from interpolations and spurious chapters. It now consists of thirty-three chapters, divided into inside, outside, and miscellaneous sections, with Kuo Hsiang's edition serving as the surviving principal version. The work is praised for its literary beauty and originality but is not considered sacred.

l: Lao Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, _Introduction._
s: Lao Tzŭ was a seventh-century B.C. Prophet who taught return of good for evil, a higher life, and the clue to human and divine things. He called this clue TAO and taught that doing nothing could allow all things to be done. His sayings influenced Chuang Tzŭ, although the existence and genuineness of the book later associated with him are disputed.

l: Confucian school, Chuang Tzŭ, _Introduction._
s: The Confucian school emphasized duty to one's neighbour, charitableness, justice, sincerity, and fortitude. Chuang Tzŭ wrote against it and sought to resist the materialism he associated with Confucian teachings.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, _Introduction._
s: TAO is the name Lao Tzŭ gave to the clue to all things human and divine. It is explained metaphorically as a way rather than a literal road, and later Taoism is described as having moved far from Lao Tzŭ's pure TAO.

l: The Way, Chuang Tzŭ, _Introduction._
s: The Way is the metaphorical meaning of TAO in Lao Tzŭ's teachings. It refers to the clue to all things human and divine rather than to a road upon which men walk.

l: Inaction, Chuang Tzŭ, _Introduction._
s: Inaction is the wondrous doctrine on which Lao Tzŭ's claim to immortality is said to rest. It teaches that doing nothing allows all things to be done and that the soft and weak can overcome the hard and strong.

l: Confucius, Chuang Tzŭ, _Introduction._
s: Confucius taught practical ethics centered on duty to one's neighbour, charitableness, justice, sincerity, and fortitude. He did not address a God, a soul, or an unseen world, and Chuang Tzŭ placed sayings found in The Tao-Tê-Ching into Confucius's mouth.

l: materialism, Chuang Tzŭ, _Introduction._
s: Materialism is presented as the tendency against which Chuang Tzŭ raised a powerful cry. He sought to stem the materialism associated with Confucian teachings, although the text says he failed to persuade the calculating Chinese nation to accept Inaction.

l: the _Tao-Tê-Ching_, Chuang Tzŭ, _Introduction._
s: The Tao-Tê-Ching is described as a later compilation, probably pieced together from recorded sayings and conversations of Lao Tzŭ. It contains genuine sayings attributed to Lao Tzŭ as well as material he never said, and it is said to reflect the corruption of pure TAO by alchemistic research and searches for the elixir of life. The text argues that it can only be called a sacred book by a severe stretch of courtesy.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: The Note on the Philosophy of Chaps. i-vii., written by the REV. AUBREY MOORE, compares Chuang Tzŭ’s philosophy with Greek philosophy, especially the thought of Heracleitus. It discusses relativity, the limitations of sense knowledge, the Identity of Contraries, and the movement from idealism toward mysticism. It presents Tao as an eternal principle comparable in some respects to Heracleitus’s Λόγος, while contrasting Taoism with Confucianism and relating Taoist inwardness to Christianity. The note also considers the roles of Aristotle, Socrates, Emperor Yao, Confucius, and Lao Tzŭ in these philosophical comparisons.

l: REV. AUBREY MOORE, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: REV. AUBREY MOORE writes the note, presenting parallels between Chuang Tzŭ and Western philosophy while acknowledging the difficulty of interpreting Chinese thought through Western preconceptions.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: Chuang Tzŭ is presented as an idealist and mystic who criticizes ordinary judgments, sense knowledge, utilitarian standards, external appearances, and individual selfhood. His philosophy teaches withdrawal from action and reputation, absorption in Tao, and the identity of apparent contraries.

l: Note on the Philosophy of Chaps. i-vii, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: The note compares Chuang Tzŭ’s philosophy with Greek philosophy and discusses its critical, idealist, mystical, and antinomian elements. It emphasizes parallels between Chuang Tzŭ and Heracleitus without claiming direct derivation.

l: Western philosophy, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: Western philosophy supplies the comparative framework for interpreting Chuang Tzŭ, especially through discussions of idealism, scepticism, mysticism, Aristotle, Heracleitus, and Christianity.

l: East and West, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: East and West are compared through parallel developments in philosophical reasoning, with the note urging readers to recognize resemblances without assuming theories of derivation.

l: Aristotle, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: Aristotle is associated with the doctrine of the mean, which the note compares with the Confucianist Doctrine of the Mean attributed to Tzŭ Tzŭ.

l: Confucianism, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: Confucianism is described as a practical system concerned with action, effort, benevolence, unselfishness, ceremonies, music, and worldly wisdom. Taoism is presented as reacting against its limitation to the finite.

l: Yao, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: Emperor Yao is said to have been willing to abdicate in favor of a hermit. He is also compared with Heracleitus, who allegedly abdicated in his brother’s favor.

l: Socrates, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: Socrates is mentioned as having been called a Sophist because of his destructive criticism and continual challenge to popular views.

l: Heracleitus, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: Heracleitus is presented as the closest Greek parallel to Chuang Tzŭ, teaching that all things are one, that contraries coexist, and that sense knowledge and common views are unreliable. Unlike Chuang Tzŭ, he is said not to have fully developed mystical flight from the world or absorption in God.

l: idealism of Lao Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: Idealism is described as turning away from the outward world toward the inward voice when the relativity of sense knowledge is recognized. Chuang Tzŭ is identified with idealism through his rejection of utilitarianism and external activity.

l: scepticism, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: Scepticism is presented as one possible conclusion from the relativity of sense knowledge, holding that real knowledge is impossible when sense is the only organ of knowledge. Chuang Tzŭ is explicitly distinguished from the sceptic.

l: mysticism, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: Mysticism in Chuang Tzŭ is associated with abstraction from self, passive union with Tao, indifference to life and death, and becoming a vehicle of higher illumination. The note also warns that mystical utterances can produce antinomianism if taken literally.

l: relativity, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: Relativity is illustrated through the changing judgments of size, space, and time, such as the Rukh, the cicada, P'êng Tsu, and the mushroom of a day. The note says this doctrine can lead either to scepticism or idealism.

l: sense knowledge, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: Sense knowledge is treated as relative and inadequate for reaching truth. Chuang Tzŭ and Heracleitus are both said to criticize reliance on the senses and common appearances.

l: TAO, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: Tao is presented as the eternal principle underlying heaven, earth, spiritual beings, the universe, natural order, law, and universal reason. Chuang Tzŭ teaches that attaining Tao requires freedom from self, action, reputation, duty, ceremonies, and conscious effort.

l: Identity of Contraries, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: The Identity of Contraries describes the sage’s vision that distinctions such as subjective and objective, positive and negative, beauty and ugliness, construction and destruction, and good and evil are unified from the standpoint of Tao.

l: Confucius, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: Confucius appears as a teacher associated with Confucian duty and practical wisdom, but in one passage he speaks as a disciple of Lao Tzŭ and teaches the fasting of the heart. Chuang Tzŭ also contrasts Confucius with a mutilated criminal judged to be the greater man.

l: Lao Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: Lao Tzŭ is described as older than Confucius and as having possibly met him. The note questions whether Quietism and the glorification of Inaction were as prominent in Lao Tzŭ’s undisputed teachings as they became in Chuang Tzŭ.

l: Christianity, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: Christianity is said to share with Chuang Tzŭ’s philosophy an emphasis on inwardness and resistance to limiting human life and knowledge to visible things.

l: Λόγος, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: Λόγος is compared with Tao as an eternal principle identified in Heracleitus with Necessity, Fate, Mind, Justice, Law, and universal Reason. The note says both Λόγος and Tao are difficult to relate precisely to God.

l: Taoism, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: Taoism is contrasted with Confucianism as a system seeking the Absolute, Infinite, and Eternal rather than worldly wisdom and practical duty. Its mysticism is said to have developed as an opposition to established Confucianism, while its later debased form is mentioned without further explanation.

l: Greek philosophy, Chuang Tzŭ, _Note on the Philosophy of Chaps._ i-vii.
s: Greek philosophy is used to identify parallels with Chuang Tzŭ, including the doctrine of relativity, the contrast between sense and reason, Aristotle’s doctrine of the mean, Parmenides, Heracleitus, Plato, and later mystical thinkers.

l: Chuang Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, The triumph of Confucianism in the centuries which intervened between
s: The unit examines the relationship between Confucianism and Taoism, especially how Confucius is portrayed in the writings of Chuang Tzŭ and Lieh Tzŭ. It proposes that Lao Tzŭ and Confucius may have been philosophically closer than later Taoism and Confucianism, with one emphasizing the ideal and inward TAO and the other practical social duties. It argues that the two traditions diverged over time, with Confucianism becoming established and Taoism responding as a mystical and dissenting movement. The writer also notes a possible parallel between Chuang Tzŭ's teaching and Heracleitus, while acknowledging dependence on translation and the risk of Western interpretive bias.

l: Confucianism, Chuang Tzŭ, The triumph of Confucianism in the centuries which intervened between
s: Confucianism is described as triumphing or becoming established over time, while its practical and utilitarian view of TAO diverges from Taoism's mystical emphasis. Mencius regards Lao Tzŭ as a heresiarch, and Confucianism's dominance leaves Taoists as dissenters.

l: Taoism, Chuang Tzŭ, The triumph of Confucianism in the centuries which intervened between
s: Taoism is presented as antagonistic toward Confucianism in the writings of Chuang Tzŭ and Lieh Tzŭ, while sometimes using Confucius to advance Taoist arguments. It increasingly becomes mystical and adopts a policy of protest as Confucianism becomes established.

l: Lao Tzŭ, Chuang Tzŭ, The triumph of Confucianism in the centuries which intervened between
s: Lao Tzŭ is portrayed as cultivating the TAO and virtue, seeking to remain concealed and unknown. His view of the TAO is associated with the hidden and inward, in contrast with Confucius' practical emphasis, though the unit suggests the two may originally have been philosophically close.

l: Confucius, Chuang Tzŭ, The triumph of Confucianism in the centuries which intervened between
s: Confucius is sometimes represented as supporting Taoist arguments, including by giving a Taoist refutation of Confucianist doctrines defended by Yen Hui. Elsewhere he is ridiculed as lacking sense, and a traditional episode describes him visiting Lao Tzŭ to ask about the TAO.
